entries.2116fbac636347393e93350041262488c19d6c6d: <div sID="gen11317" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="50" osisID="Ps.50" sID="Ps.50"/> <div eID="gen11317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11318" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11319" type="x-p"/> This psalm, as the former, is a psalm of instruction, not of prayer or praise; it is a psalm of reproof and admonition, in singing which we are to teach and admonish one another. In the foregoing psalm, after a general demand of attention, God by his prophet deals (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.3">ver. 3</reference>) with the children of this world, to convince them of their sin and folly in setting their hearts upon the wealth of this world; in this psalm, after a like preface, he deals with those that were, in profession, the church's children, to convince them of their sin and folly in placing their religion in ritual services, while they neglected practical godliness; and this is as sure a way to ruin as the other. This psalm is intended, 1. As a proof to the carnal Jews, both those that rested in the external performances of their religion, and were remiss in the more excellent duties of prayer and praise, and those that expounded the law to others, but lived wicked lives themselves. 2. As a prediction of the abolishing of the ceremonial law, and of the introducing of a spiritual way of worship in and by the kingdom of the Messiah, <reference osisRef="John.4.23-John.4.24">John iv. 23, 24</reference>. 3. As a representation of the day of judgment, in which God will call men to an account concerning their observance of those things which they have thus been taught; men shall be judged "according to what is written in the books;" and therefore Christ is fitly represented speaking as a Judge, then when he speaks as a Lawgiver. Here is, I. The glorious appearance of the Prince that gives law and judgment, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.1-Ps.50.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. Instruction given to his worshippers, to turn their sacrifices into prayers, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.7-Ps.50.15">ver. 7-15</reference>. III. A rebuke to those that pretend to worship God, but live in disobedience to his commands (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.16-Ps.50.20">ver. 16-20</reference>), their doom read (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.21-Ps.50.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>), and warning given to all to look to their conversation as well as to their devotions, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">ver. 23</reference>. These instructions and admonitions we must take to ourselves, and give to one another, in singing this psalm.
entries.eedcb66b41d00d4c168100a78d1ad3caaaa1f1d5: <div eID="gen11319" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11318" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Majesty of Messiah.</title> <div sID="gen11320" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The mighty God, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , hath spoken, and called the earth from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof. <hi type="super">2</hi> Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God hath shined. <hi type="super">3</hi> Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him. <hi type="super">4</hi> He shall call to the heavens from above, and to the earth, that he may judge his people. <hi type="super">5</hi> Gather my saints together unto me; those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the heavens shall declare his righteousness: for God <hi type="italic">is</hi> judge himself. Selah. <div eID="gen11320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11321" type="x-p"/> It is probable that Asaph was not only the chief musician, who was to put a tune to this psalm, but that he was himself the penman of it; for we read that in Hezekiah's time they praised God <hi type="italic">in the words of David and of Asaph the seer,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.30">2 Chron. xxix. 30</reference>. Here is, <div eID="gen11321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11322" type="x-p"/> I. The court called, in the name of the King of kings (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">The mighty God, even the Lord, hath spoken</hi>—El, Elohim, Jehovah, the God of infinite power justice and mercy, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. God is the Judge, the Son of God came for judgement into the world, and the Holy Ghost is the Spirit of judgment. All the earth is called to attend, not only because the controversy God had with his people Israel for their hypocrisy and ingratitude might safely be referred to any man of reason (nay, let the house of Israel itself <hi type="italic">judge between God and his vineyard,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.5.3">Isa. v. 3</reference>), but because all the children of men are concerned to know the right way of worshipping God, in spirit and in truth, because when the kingdom of the Messiah should be set up all should be instructed in the evangelical worship, and invited to join in it (see <reference osisRef="Mal.1.11">Mal. i. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.34">Acts x. 34</reference>), and because in the day of final judgment all nations shall be gathered together to receive their doom, and every man shall give an account of himself unto God. <div eID="gen11322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11323" type="x-p"/> II. The judgment set, and the Judge taking his seat. As, when God gave the law to Israel in the wilderness, it is said, <hi type="italic">He came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir, and shone forth from Mount Paran, and came with ten thousands of his saints, and then from his right hand went a fiery law</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">Deut. xxxiii. 2</reference>), so, with allusion to that, when God comes to reprove them for their hypocrisy, and to send forth his gospel to supersede the legal institutions, it is said here, 1. That <hi type="italic">he shall shine out of Zion,</hi> as then from the top of Sinai, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.2">v. 2</reference>. Because in Zion his oracle was now fixed, thence his judgments upon that provoking people denounced, and thence the orders issued for the execution of them (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.1">Joel ii. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blow you the trumpet in Zion.</hi> Sometimes there are more than ordinary appearances of God's presence and power working with and by his word and ordinances, for the convincing of men's consciences and the reforming and refining of his church; and then God, who always dwells in Zion, may be said to <hi type="italic">shine out of Zion.</hi> Moreover, he may be said to <hi type="italic">shine out of Zion</hi> because the gospel, which set up spiritual worship, was to <hi type="italic">go forth from Mount Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.2">Mic. iv. 2</reference>), and the preachers of it were to <hi type="italic">begin at Jerusalem</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">Luke xxiv. 47</reference>), and Christians are said to come unto Mount Zion, to receive their instructions, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">Heb. xii. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.28">28</reference>. Zion is here called <hi type="italic">the perfection of beauty,</hi> because it was the holy hill; and holiness is indeed the perfection of beauty. 2. That he <hi type="italic">shall come, and not keep silence,</hi> shall no longer seem to wink at the sins of men, as he had done (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.21">v. 21</reference>), but shall show his displeasure at them, and shall also cause that mystery to be published to the world by his holy apostles which had long <hi type="italic">lain hid, that the Gentiles should be fellow-heirs</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.5-Eph.3.6">Eph. iii. 5, 6</reference>) and that the partition-wall of the ceremonial law should be taken down; this shall now no longer be concealed. In the great day <hi type="italic">our God shall come and shall not keep silence,</hi> but shall make those to hear his judgment that would not hearken to his law. 3. That his appearance should be very majestic and terrible: <hi type="italic">A fire shall devour before him.</hi> The fire of his judgments shall make way for the rebukes of his word, in order to the awakening of the hypocritical nation of the Jews, that the sinners in Zion, being afraid of that devouring fire (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">Isa. xxxiii. 14</reference>), might be startled out of their sins. When his gospel kingdom was to be set up Christ <hi type="italic">came to send fire on the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.49">Luke xii. 49</reference>. The Spirit was given in cloven tongues as of fire, introduced by a rushing mighty wind, which was very tempestuous, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.2-Acts.2.3">Acts ii. 2, 3</reference>. And in the last judgment Christ shall come in flaming fire, <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.8">2 Thess. i. 8</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Dan.7.9">Dan. vii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.27">Heb. x. 27</reference>. 4. That as on Mount Sinai he came with <hi type="italic">ten thousands of his saints,</hi> so he shall now <hi type="italic">call to the heavens from above,</hi> to take notice of this solemn process (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.4">v. 4</reference>), as Moses often <hi type="italic">called heaven and earth to witness</hi> against Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.26">Deut. iv. 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.31.28 Deut.32.21">xxxi. 28, xxxii. 1</reference>), and God by his prophets, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Isa. i. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.2">Mic. vi. 2</reference>. The equity of the judgment of the great day will be attested and applauded by heaven and earth, by saints and angels, even all the holy myriads. <div eID="gen11323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11324" type="x-p"/> III. The parties summoned (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Gather my saints together unto me.</hi> This may be understood either, 1. Of saints indeed: "Let them be gathered to God through Christ; let the few pious Israelites be set by themselves;" for to them the following denunciations of wrath do not belong; rebukes to hypocrites ought not to be terrors to the upright. When God will reject the services of those that only offered sacrifice, resting in the outside of the performance, he will graciously accept those who, in sacrificing, <hi type="italic">make a covenant with him,</hi> and so attend to and answer the end of the institution of sacrifices. The design of the preaching of the gospel, and the setting up of Christ's kingdom, was to gather together in one the children of God, <reference osisRef="John.11.52">John xi. 52</reference>. And at the second coming of Jesus Christ all his saints shall be <hi type="italic">gathered together unto him</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.1">2 Thess. ii. 1</reference>) to be assessors with him in the judgment; for <hi type="italic">the saints shall judge the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2">1 Cor. vi. 2</reference>. Now it is here given as a character of the saints that they have made a covenant with God by sacrifice. Note, (1.) Those only shall be gathered to God as his saints who have, in sincerity, covenanted with him, who have taken him to be their God and given up themselves to him to be his people, and thus have joined themselves unto the Lord. (2.) It is only by sacrifice, by Christ the great sacrifice (from whom all the legal sacrifices derived what value they had), that we poor sinners can covenant with God so as to be accepted of him. There must be an atonement made for the breach of the first covenant before we can be admitted again into covenant. Or, 2. It may be understood of saints in profession, such as the people of Israel were, who are called <hi type="italic">a kingdom of priests</hi> and <hi type="italic">a holy nation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Exod. xix. 6</reference>. They were, as a body politic, taken into covenant with God, the covenant of peculiarity; and it was done with great solemnity, <hi type="italic">by sacrifice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.24.8">Exod. xxiv. 8</reference>. "Let them come and hear what God has to say to them; let them receive the reproofs God sends them now by his prophets, and the gospel he will, in due time, send them by his Son, which shall supersede the ceremonial law. If these be slighted, let them expect to hear from God another way, and to be judged by that word which they will not be ruled by." <div eID="gen11324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11325" type="x-p"/> IV. The issue of this solemn trial foretold (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The heavens shall declare his righteousness,</hi> those heavens that were called to be witnesses to the trial (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.4">v. 4</reference>); the <hi type="italic">people in heaven shall say, Hallelujah. True and righteous are his judgments,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.1-Rev.19.2">Rev. xix. 1, 2</reference>. The righteousness of God in all the rebukes of his word and providence, in the establishment of his gospel (which <hi type="italic">brings in an everlasting righteousness,</hi> and in which <hi type="italic">the righteousness of God is revealed</hi>), and especially in the judgment of the great day, is what the heavens will declare; that is, 1. It will be universally known, and proclaimed to all the world. <hi type="italic">As the heavens declare the glory,</hi> the wisdom and power, of God the Creator (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.1">Ps. xix. 1</reference>), so they shall no less openly declare the glory, the justice and righteousness, of God the <hi type="italic">Judge;</hi> and so loudly do they proclaim both that <hi type="italic">there is no speech nor language where their voice is not heard,</hi> as it follows there, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.3">v. 3</reference>. 2. It will be incontestably owned and proved; who can deny what the heavens declare? Even sinners' own consciences will subscribe to it, and hell as well as heaven will be forced to acknowledge the righteousness of God. The reason given is, <hi type="italic">for God is Judge himself,</hi> and therefore, (1.) He will be just; for it is impossible he should do any wrong to any of his creatures, he never did, nor ever will. When men are employed to judge for him they may do unjustly; but, when he is Judge himself, there can be no injustice done. <hi type="italic">Is God unrighteous, who takes vengeance?</hi> The apostle, for this reason, startles at the thought of it; <hi type="italic">God forbid! for then how shall God judge the world?</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.5-Rom.3.6">Rom. iii. 5, 6</reference>. These decisions will be perfectly just, for against them there will lie no exception, and from them there will lie no appeal. (2.) He will be justified; <hi type="italic">God is Judge,</hi> and therefore he will not only execute justice, but he will oblige all to own it; for he <hi type="italic">will be clear when he judges,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.51.4">Ps. li. 4</reference>.
entries.fb7cf9b5c3a47342f5b5674158a3386af74d29bd: <div eID="gen11325" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Inefficacy of Legal Sacrifices.</title> <div sID="gen11326" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify against thee: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> God, <hi type="italic">even</hi> thy God. <hi type="super">8</hi> I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices or thy burnt offerings, <hi type="italic">to have been</hi> continually before me. <hi type="super">9</hi> I will take no bullock out of thy house, <hi type="italic">nor</hi> he goats out of thy folds. <hi type="super">10</hi> For every beast of the forest <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the cattle upon a thousand hills. <hi type="super">11</hi> I know all the fowls of the mountains: and the wild beasts of the field <hi type="italic">are</hi> mine. <hi type="super">12</hi> If I were hungry, I would not tell thee: for the world <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine, and the fulness thereof. <hi type="super">13</hi> Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? <hi type="super">14</hi> Offer unto God thanksgiving; and pay thy vows unto the most High: <hi type="super">15</hi> And call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me. <div eID="gen11326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11327" type="x-p"/> God is here dealing with those that placed all their religion in the observances of the ceremonial law, and thought those sufficient. <div eID="gen11327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11328" type="x-p"/> I. He lays down the original contract between him and Israel, in which they had avouched him to be their God, and he them to be his people, and so both parties were agreed (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hear, O my people! and I will speak.</hi> Note, It is justly expected that whatever others doe, when he speaks, his people should give ear; who will, if they do not? And then we may comfortably expect that God will speak to us when we are ready to hear what he says; even when he testifies against us in the rebukes and threatenings of his word and providences we must be forward to hear what he says, to hear even <hi type="italic">the rod and him that has appointed it.</hi> <div eID="gen11328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11329" type="x-p"/> II. He puts a slight upon the legal sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.8-Ps.50.13">v. 8</reference>, &c. Now, <div eID="gen11329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11330" type="x-p"/> 1. This may be considered as looking back to the use of these under the law. God had a controversy with the Jews; but what was the ground of the controversy? Not their neglect of the ceremonial institutions; no, they had not been wanting in the observance of them, their burnt-offerings had been continually before God, they took a pride in them, and hoped by their offerings to procure a dispensation for their lusts, as the adulterous woman, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.14">Prov. vii. 14</reference>. Their constant sacrifices, they thought, would both expiate and excuse their neglect of the weightier matters of the law. Nay, if they had, in some degree, neglected these institutions, yet that should not have been the cause of God's quarrel with them, for it was but a small offence in comparison with the immoralities of their conversation. They thought God was mightily beholden to them for the many sacrifices they had brought to his altar, and that they had made him very much their debtor by them, as if he could not h have maintained his numerous family of priests without their contributions; but God here shows them the contrary, (1.) That he did not need their sacrifices. What occasion had he for their bullocks and goats who has the command of all <hi type="italic">the beasts of the forest,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">cattle upon a thousand hills</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.9-Ps.50.10">v. 9, 10</reference>), has an incontestable propriety in them and dominion over them, has them all always under his eye and within his reach, and can make what use he pleases of them; they all wait on him, and are all at his disposal? <reference osisRef="Ps.104.27-Ps.104.29">Ps. civ. 27-29</reference>. Can we add any thing to his store whose all the wild fowl and wild beasts are, the world itself and the fulness thereof? <reference osisRef="Ps.50.11-Ps.50.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. God's infinite self-sufficiency proves our utter insufficiency to add any thing to him. (2.) That he could not be benefited by their sacrifices. Their goodness, of this kind, could not possibly extend to him, nor, if they were in this matter righteous, was he the better (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Will I eat the flesh of bulls?</hi> It is as absurd to think that their sacrifices could, of themselves, and by virtue of any innate excellency in them, add any pleasure of praise to God, as it would be to imagine that an infinite Spirit could be supported by meat and drink, as our bodies are. It is said indeed of the demons whom the Gentiles worshipped that they did <hi type="italic">eat the fat of their sacrifices, and drink the wine of their drink-offerings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.38">Deut. xxxii. 38</reference>): they regaled themselves in the homage they robbed the true God of; but will the great Jehovah be thus entertained? No; <hi type="italic">to obey is better than sacrifice,</hi> and to love God and our neighbour <hi type="italic">better than all burnt-offerings,</hi> so much better that God by his prophets often told them that their sacrifices were not only not acceptable, but abominable, to him, while they lived in sin; instead of pleasing him, he looked upon them as a mockery, and therefore an affront and provocation to him; see <reference osisRef="Prov.15.8 Isa.1.11-Isa.1.23">Prov. xv. 8; Isa. i. 11, &c.</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.3">lxvi. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.20">Jer. vi. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.21">Amos v. 21</reference>. They are therefore here warned not to rest in these performances; but to conduct themselves, in all other instances, towards God as their God. <div eID="gen11330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11331" type="x-p"/> 2. This may be considered as looking forward to the abolishing of these by the gospel of Christ. Thus Dr. Hammond understands it. When God shall set up the kingdom of the Messiah he shall abolish the old way of worship by sacrifice and offerings; he will no more have those to be <hi type="italic">continually before him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">v. 8</reference>); he will no more require of his worshippers to bring him their bullocks and their goats, to be burnt upon his altar, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.9">v. 9</reference>. For indeed he never appointed this as that which he had any need of, or took any pleasure in, for, besides that all we have is his already, he has far more beasts in the forest and upon the mountains, which we know nothing of nor have any property in, than we have in our folds; but he instituted it to prefigure the great sacrifice which his own Son should in the fulness of time offer upon the cross, to make atonement for sin, and all the other spiritual sacrifices of acknowledgment with which God, through Christ, will be well pleased. <div eID="gen11331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11332" type="x-p"/> III. He directs to the best sacrifices of prayer and praise as those which, under the law, were preferred before all burn-offerings and sacrifices, and on which then the greatest stress was laid, and which now, under the gospel, come in the room of those carnal ordinances which were imposed until the times of reformation. He shows us here (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.14-Ps.50.15">v. 14, 15</reference>) what is good, and what the Lord our God requires of us, and will accept, when sacrifices are slighted and superseded. 1. We must make a penitent acknowledgment of our sins: <hi type="italic">Offer to God confession,</hi> so some read it, and understand it of the confession of sin, in order to our giving glory to God and taking shame to ourselves, that we may never return to it. <hi type="italic">A broken and contrite heart</hi> is the sacrifice which <hi type="italic">God will not despise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.51.17">Ps. li. 17</reference>. If the sin was not abandoned the sin-offering was not accepted. 2. We must give God thanks for his mercies to us: <hi type="italic">Offer to God thanksgiving,</hi> every day, often every day (<hi type="italic">seven times a day will I praise thee</hi>), and upon special occasions; and <hi type="italic">this shall please the Lord,</hi> if it come from a humble thankful heart, full of love to him and joy in him, <hi type="italic">better than an ox or bullock that has horns and hoofs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.69.30-Ps.69.31">Ps. lxix. 30, 31</reference>. 3. We must make conscience of performing our covenants with him: <hi type="italic">Pay thy vows to the Most High,</hi> forsake thy sins, and do thy duty better, pursuant to the solemn promises thou has made him to that purport. When we give God thanks for any mercy we have received we must be sure to pay the vows we made to him when we were in the pursuit of the mercy, else our thanksgivings will not be accepted. Dr. Hammond applies this to the great gospel ordinance of the eucharist, in which we are to give thanks to God for his great love in sending his Son to save us, and to pay our vows of love and duty to him, and to give alms. Instead of all the Old Testament types of a Christ to come, we have that blessed memorial of a Christ already come. 4. In the day of distress we must address ourselves to God by faithful and fervent prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Call upon me in the day of trouble,</hi> and not upon any other god. Our troubles, though we see them coming from God's hand, must drive us to him, and not drive us from him. We must thus acknowledge him in all our ways, depend upon his wisdom, power, and goodness, and refer ourselves entirely to him, and so give him glory. This is a cheaper, easier, readier way of seeking his favour than by a peace-offering, and yet more acceptable. 5. When he, in answer to our prayers, delivers us, as he has promised to do in such way and time as he shall think fit, we must glorify him, not only by a grateful mention of his favour, but by living to his praise. Thus must we keep up our communion with God, meeting him with our prayers when he afflicts us and with our praises when he delivers us.
entries.5593e7f3c1bf445f9019cc8c7aa5ed01dd9bb5f1: <div eID="gen11332" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Character of the Wicked.</title> <div sID="gen11333" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth? <hi type="super">17</hi> Seeing thou hatest instruction, and castest my words behind thee. <hi type="super">18</hi> When thou sawest a thief, then thou consentedst with him, and hast been partaker with adulterers. <hi type="super">19</hi> Thou givest thy mouth to evil, and thy tongue frameth deceit. <hi type="super">20</hi> Thou sittest <hi type="italic">and</hi> speakest against thy brother; thou slanderest thine own mother's son. <hi type="super">21</hi> These <hi type="italic">things</hi> hast thou done, and I kept silence; thou thoughtest that I was altogether <hi type="italic">such an one</hi> as thyself: <hi type="italic">but</hi> I will reprove thee, and set <hi type="italic">them</hi> in order before thine eyes. <hi type="super">22</hi> Now consider this, ye that forget God, lest I tear <hi type="italic">you</hi> in pieces, and <hi type="italic">there be</hi> none to deliver. 23 Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me: and to him that ordereth <hi type="italic">his</hi> conversation <hi type="italic">aright</hi> will I show the salvation of God. <div eID="gen11333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11334" type="x-p"/> God, by the psalmist, having instructed his people in the right way of worshipping him and keeping up their communion with him, here directs his speech to the wicked, to hypocrites, whether they were such as professed the Jewish or the Christian religion: hypocrisy is wickedness for which God will judge. Observe here, <div eID="gen11334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11335" type="x-p"/> I. The charge drawn up against them. 1. They are charged with invading and usurping the honours and privileges of religion (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">What has thou to do,</hi> O wicked man! <hi type="italic">to declare my statutes?</hi> This is a challenge to those that rare really profane, but seemingly godly, to show what title they have to the cloak of religion, and by what authority they wear it, when they use it only to cover and conceal the abominable impieties of their hearts and lives. Let them make out their claim to it if they can. Some think it points prophetically at the scribes and Pharisees that were the teachers and leaders of the Jewish church at the time when the kingdom of the Messiah, and that evangelical way of worship spoken of in the <reference osisRef="Ps.50.7-Ps.50.15">foregoing verses</reference>, were to be set up. They violently opposed that great revolution, and used all the power and interest which they had by sitting in Moses's seat to hinder it; but the account which our blessed Saviour gives of them (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.1-Matt.23.36">Matt. xxiii</reference>.), and St. Paul (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.21-Rom.2.22">Rom. ii. 21, 22</reference>), makes this expostulation here agree very well to them. They took on them to declare God's statues, but they hated Christ's instruction; and therefore what had they to do to expound the law, when they rejected the gospel? But it is applicable to all those that are practicers of iniquity, and yet professors of piety, especially if withal they be preachers of it. Note, It is very absurd in itself, and a great affront to the God of heaven, for those that are wicked and ungodly to declare his statutes and to take his covenant in their mouths. It is very possible, and too common, for those that declare God's statutes to others to live in disobedience to them themselves, and for those that take God's covenant in their mouths yet in their hearts to continue their covenant with sin and death; but they are guilty of a usurpation, they take to themselves an honour which they have no title to, and there is a day coming when they will be thrust out as intruders. <hi type="italic">Friend, how camest thou in hither?</hi> 2. They are charged with transgressing and violating the laws and precepts of religion. (1.) They are charged with a daring contempt of the word of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hatest instruction.</hi> They loved to give instruction, and to tell others what they should do, for this fed their pride and made them look great, and by this craft they got their living; but they hated to receive instruction from God himself, for that would be a check upon them and a mortification to them. "Thou hatest discipline, the reproofs of the word and the rebukes of Providence." No wonder that those who hate to be reformed hate the means of reformation. <hi type="italic">Thou castest my words behind thee.</hi> They seemed to set God's words before them, when they sat in Moses's seat, and undertook to teach others out of the law (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.19">Rom. ii. 19</reference>); but in their conversations they cast God's word behind them, and did not care for seeing that rule which they were resolved not to be ruled by. This is despising the commandment of the Lord. (2.) A close confederacy with the worst of sinners (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">When thou sawest a thief,</hi> instead of reproving him and witnessing against him, as those should do that declare God's statutes, <hi type="italic">thou consentedst with him,</hi> didst approve of his practices, and desire to be a partner with him and to share in the profits of his cursed trade; <hi type="italic">and thou hast been partaker with adulterers,</hi> hast done as they did, and encouraged them to go on in their wicked courses, hast done these things and hast <hi type="italic">had pleasure in those that do them,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Rom.1.32">Rom. i. 32</reference>. (3.) A constant persisting in the worst of tongue-sins (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou givest thy mouth to evil,</hi> not only allowest thyself in, but addictest thyself wholly to, all manner of evil-speaking." [1.] Lying: <hi type="italic">Thy tongue frames deceit,</hi> which denotes contrivance and deliberation in lying. It <hi type="italic">knits</hi> or <hi type="italic">links</hi> deceit, so some. One lie begets another, and one fraud requires another to cover it. [2.] Slandering (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou sittest, and speakest against thy brother,</hi> dost basely abuse and misrepresent him, magisterially judge and censure him, and pass sentence upon him, as if you wert his master to whom he must stand or fall, whereas he is thy brother, as good as thou art, and upon the level with thee, for he is <hi type="italic">thy own mother's son.</hi> He is thy near relation, whom thou oughtest to love, to vindicate, and stand up for, if others abused him; yet thou dost thyself abuse him, whose faults thou oughtest to cover and make the best of; if really he had done amiss, yet thou dost most falsely and unjustly charge him with that which he is innocent of; <hi type="italic">thou sittest</hi> and doest this, as a judge upon the bench, with authority; thou sittest in the seat of the scornful, to deride and backbite those whom thou oughtest to respect and be kind to." Those that do ill themselves commonly delight in speaking ill of others. <div eID="gen11335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11336" type="x-p"/> II. The proof of this charge (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.21">v. 21</reference>): "<hi type="italic">These things thou hast done;</hi> the fact is too plain to be denied, the fault too bad to be excused; these things God knows, and thy own heart knows, thou hast done." The sins of sinners will be proved upon them, beyond contradiction, in the judgment of the great day: "<hi type="italic">I will reprove thee,</hi> or convince thee, so that thou shalt have not one word to say for thyself." The day is coming when impenitent sinners will have their mouths for ever stopped and be struck speechless. What confusion will they be filled with when God shall set their sins in order before their eyes! They would not see their sins to their humiliation, but cast them behind their backs, covered them, and endeavoured to forget them, nor would they suffer their own consciences to put them in mind of them; but the day is coming when God will make them see their sins to their everlasting shame and terror; he will set them in order, original sin, actual sins, sins against the law, sins against the gospel, against the first table, against the second table, sins of childhood and youth, of riper age, and old age. He will set them in order, as the witnesses are set in order, and called in order, against the criminal, and asked what they have to say against him. <div eID="gen11336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11337" type="x-p"/> III. The Judge's patience, and the sinner's abuse of that patience: "<hi type="italic">I kept silence,</hi> did not give thee any disturbance in thy sinful way, but let thee alone to take thy course; sentence against thy evil works was respited, and not executed speedily." Note, The patience of God is very great towards provoking sinners. He sees their sins and hates them; it would be neither difficulty nor damage to him to punish them, and yet he waits to be gracious and gives them space to repent, that he may render them inexcusable if they repent not. His patience is the more wonderful because the sinner makes such an ill use of it: "<hi type="italic">Thou thoughtest that I was altogether such a one as thyself,</hi> as weak and forgetful as thyself, as false to my word as thyself, nay, as much a friend to sin as thyself." Sinners take God's silence for consent and his patience for connivance; and therefore the longer they are reprieved the more are their hearts hardened; but, if they turn not, they shall be made to see their error when it is too late, and that the God they provoke is just, and holy, and terrible, and not such a one as themselves. <div eID="gen11337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11338" type="x-p"/> IV. The fair warning given of the dreadful doom of hypocrites (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Now consider this, you that forget God,</hi> consider that God knows and keeps account of all your sins, that he will call you to an account for them, that patience abused will turn into the greater wrath, that though you forget God and your duty to him he will not forget you and your rebellions against him: consider this in time, before it be too late; for if these things be not considered, and the consideration of them improved, he will <hi type="italic">tear you in pieces, and there will be none to deliver.</hi>" It is the doom of hypocrites to be <hi type="italic">cut asunder,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.51">Matt. xxiv. 51</reference>. Note, 1. Forgetfulness of God is at the bottom of all the wickedness of the wicked. Those that know God, and yet do not obey him, do certainly forget him. 2. Those that forget God forget themselves; and it will never be right with them till they consider, and so recover themselves. Consideration is the first step towards conversion. 3. Those that will not consider the warnings of God's word will certainly be torn in pieces by the executions of his wrath. 4. When God comes to tear sinners in pieces, there is no delivering them out of his hand. They cannot deliver themselves, nor can any friend they have in the world deliver them. <div eID="gen11338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11339" type="x-p"/> V. Full instructions given to us all how to prevent this fearful doom. Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter; we have it, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">v. 23</reference>, which directs us what to do that we may attain our chief end. 1. Man's chief end is to glorify God, and we are here told that <hi type="italic">whoso offers praise glorifies him;</hi> whether he be Jew or Gentile, those spiritual sacrifices shall be accepted from him. We must praise God, and we must sacrifice praise, direct it to God, as every sacrifice was directed; put it into the hands of the priest, our Lord Jesus, who is also the altar; see that it be made by fire, sacred fire, that it be kindled with the flame of holy and devout affection; we must be fervent in spirit, praising the Lord. This he is pleased, in infinite condescension, to interpret as glorifying him. Hereby we give him the glory due to his name and do what we can to advance the interests of his kingdom among men. 2. Man's chief end, in conjunction with this, is to enjoy God; and we are here told that those who <hi type="italic">order their conversation aright shall see his salvation.</hi> (1.) It is not enough for us to offer praise, but we must withal order our conversation aright. Thanksgiving is good, but thanks-living is better. (2.) Those that would have their conversation right must take care and pains to order it, to dispose it according to rule, to understand their way and to direct it. (3.) Those that take care of their conversation make sure their salvation; them God will make to see his salvation, for it is a salvation ready to be revealed; he will make them to see it and enjoy it, to see it, and to see themselves happy for ever in it. Note, The right ordering of the conversation is the only way, and it is a sure way, to obtain the great salvation.  <chapter eID="Ps.50"/> <div eID="gen11339" type="x-p"/>

entries.31b793abc4874b7bbcf817b966e410e2ba6eddf3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6043"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 50</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.50.1-Ps.50.23">Psa 50:1-23</reference>. In the grandeur and solemnity of a divine judgment, God is introduced as instructing men in the nature of true worship, exposing hypocrisy, warning the wicked, and encouraging the pious.</title> <div sID="gen9225" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6043"/>1-4. The description of this majestic appearance of God resembles that of His giving the law (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.19.16">Ex 19:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.20.18">20:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.1">De 32:1</reference>). <div eID="gen9225" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8f40a41f73e4a60c286fcda8c6fc5a207226c23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6045"/><div sID="gen9228" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6045"/><hi type="bold">5. my saints--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen9228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made--</hi>literally, "cut"<div eID="gen9229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9230" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a covenant, &c.--</hi>alluding to the dividing of a victim of sacrifice, by which covenants were ratified, the parties passing between the divided portions (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.15.10">Ge 15:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">18</reference>). <div eID="gen9230" type="x-p"/>
entries.330b7f3479e03e2a6f20ada0a560080f2e9a780f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6046"/><div sID="gen9231" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6046"/>6. The inhabitants of heaven, who well know God's character, attest His righteousness as a judge. <div eID="gen9231" type="x-p"/>
entries.19ec5d41675922630b1a8ee88e96e8fedaef5dbf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6047"/><div sID="gen9232" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6047"/><hi type="bold">7. I will testify--</hi>that is, for failure to worship aught.<div eID="gen9232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy God--</hi>and so, by covenant as well as creation, entitled to a pure worship. <div eID="gen9233" type="x-p"/>
entries.86dfd3c402881a0fcc126515016d8deebe1ed26a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6048"/><div sID="gen9234" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6048"/><hi type="bold">8-15. However scrupulous in external worship, it was offered as if they conferred an obligation in giving God His own, and with a degrading view of Him as needing it [Psa 50:9-13]. Reproving them for such foolish and blasphemous notions, He teaches them to offer, or literally, "sacrifice," thanksgiving, and pay, or perform, their vows--</hi>that is, to bring, with the external symbolical service, the homage of the heart, and faith, penitence, and love. To this is added an invitation to seek, and a promise to afford, all needed help in trouble. <div eID="gen9234" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5a0f0bcad532de8026ff056670c0a9fc25a32c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6049"/><div sID="gen9235" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6049"/><hi type="bold">16-20. the wicked--</hi>that is, the formalists, as now exposed, and who lead vicious lives (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.2.21">Ro 2:21</reference>, 23). They are unworthy to use even the words of God's law. Their hypocrisy and vice are exposed by illustrations from sins against the seventh, eighth, and ninth commandments. <div eID="gen9235" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed2a1a1daee6686aa45871ce0606b95d0aadd201: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6050"/><div sID="gen9236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6050"/>21-22. God, no longer (even in appearance) disregarding such, exposes their sins and threatens a terrible punishment. <div eID="gen9236" type="x-p"/>
entries.397124d122a45105be7400839474cb550977237d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6052"/><div sID="gen9238" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6052"/><hi type="bold">23. offereth praise--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.50.14">Psa 50:14</reference>), so that the external worship is a true index of the heart.<div eID="gen9238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ordereth ... aright--</hi>acts in a straight, right manner, opposed to turning aside (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.5">Psa 25:5</reference>). In such, pure worship and a pure life evince their true piety, and they will enjoy God's presence and favor. <chapter eID="Ps.50"/>

entries.4dd941a686658d350173a4d4b7330cc09c5c0f43: <div eID="gen20205" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20206" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20207" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20207" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20206" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20208" type="x-p"/> God, the Sovereign Judge, cites before his throne all his people, and the priests and the judges, <reference osisRef="Psa.50.1-Psa.50.6">Psa 50:1-6</reference>; and reproaches them for their vain confidence in the sacrifices they had offered, <reference osisRef="Psa.50.7-Psa.50.13">Psa 50:7-13</reference>; and shows them the worship he requires, <reference osisRef="Psa.50.14">Psa 50:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.50.15">Psa 50:15</reference>; and then enters into a particular detail of their hypocrisy, injustice, and union with scandalous transgressors; all of whom he threatens with heavy judwments, <reference osisRef="Psa.50.16-Psa.50.22">Psa 50:16-22</reference>. The blessedrusss of him who worships God aright, and walks unblamably, <reference osisRef="Psa.50.23">Psa 50:23</reference>. <div eID="gen20208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20209" type="x-p"/> In the title this is said to be A Psalm of Asaph. There are twelve that go under his name; and most probably he was author of each, for he was of high repute in the days of David, and is mentioned second to him as a composer of psalms: Moreover Hezekiah the king, and the princes, commanded the Levites to sing praise unto the Lord, with the WordS of David, and of Asaph the Seer. His band, sons or companions, were also eminent in the days of David, as we learn from 1 Chronicles 25, etc. Asaph himself was one of the musicians who sounded with cymbals of brass, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19">1Chr 15:19</reference>. And he is mentioned with great respect, <reference osisRef="Neh.12.46">Neh 12:46</reference> : And in the days of David and Asaph of old there were Chief of the Singers, and Songs of Praise and Thanksgiving unto God. He was certainly a prophetic man: he is called a seer - one on whom the Spirit of God rested; and seems from this, his education, and natural talent to be well qualified to compose hymns or psaims in the honor of God. Persons capable of judging, on a comparison of those Psalms attributed to Asaph with those known to be of David, have found a remarkable difference in the style. The style of David is more polished, flowing, correct, and majestic, than that of Asaph, which is more stiff and obscure. He has been compared to Persius and to Horace; he is keen, full of reprehensions, and his subjects are generally of the doleful kind; which was probably caused by his living in times in which there was great corruption of manners, and much of the displeasure of God either theatened or manifested. It is not known on what particular occasion this Psalm was written; but at most times it was suitable to the state of the Jewish Church. <div eID="gen20209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20210" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20211" type="x-p"/> The mighty God, even the Lord, hath spoken - Here the essential names of God are used: אל אלהים יהוה El, Elohim, Yehovah, hath spoken. The six first verses of this Psalm seem to contain a description of the great judgment: to any minor consideration or fact it seems impossible, with any propriety, to restrain them. In this light I shall consider this part of the Psalm, and show: - <div eID="gen20211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20212" type="x-p"/> First, The preparatives to the coming of the great Judge. El Elohim Jehovah hath spoken, and called the earth - all the children of men from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof. Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, (מכלל יפי michlal yophi, the beauty where all perfection is comprised), God hath shined, <reference osisRef="Psa.50.1">Psa 50:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.50.2">Psa 50:2</reference>. <div eID="gen20212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20213" type="x-p"/> 1. He has sent his Spirit to convince men of sin, righteousness, and judgment. <div eID="gen20213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20214" type="x-p"/> 2. He has sent his Word; has made a revelation of himself; and has declared both his law and his Gospel to mankind: "Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God hath shined," <reference osisRef="Psa.50.2">Psa 50:2</reference>. For out of Zion the law was to go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa 2:3</reference>. <div eID="gen20214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20215" type="x-p"/> Secondly, The accompaniments. <div eID="gen20215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20216" type="x-p"/> 1. His approach is proclaimed, <reference osisRef="Psa.50.3">Psa 50:3</reference> : "Our God shall come." <div eID="gen20216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20217" type="x-p"/> 2. The trumpet proclaims his approach: "He shall not keep silence." <div eID="gen20217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20218" type="x-p"/> 3. Universal nature shall be shaken, and the earth and its works be burnt up: "A fire shall devour before him and it shall be very tempestuous round about him," <reference osisRef="Psa.50.3">Psa 50:3</reference>. <div eID="gen20218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20219" type="x-p"/> Thirdly, The witnesses are summoned and collected, and collected from all quarters; some from heaven, and some from earth. <div eID="gen20219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20220" type="x-p"/> 1. Guardian angels. <div eID="gen20220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20221" type="x-p"/> 2. Human associates: "He shall call to the heavens from above, and to the earth, that he may judge his people," <reference osisRef="Psa.50.4">Psa 50:4</reference>. <div eID="gen20221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20222" type="x-p"/> Fourthly, The procedure. As far as it respects the righteous, orders are issued: "Gather my saints," those who are saved from their sins and made holy, "together unto me." And that the word saints might not be misunderstood it is explained by "those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice;" those who have entered into union with God, through the sacrificial offering of the Lord Jesus Christ. All the rest are passed over in silence. We are told who they are that shall enter into the joy of their Lord, viz., only the saints, those who have made a covenant with God by sacrifice. All, therefore, who do not answer this description are excluded from glory. <div eID="gen20222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20223" type="x-p"/> Fifthly, The final issue: all the angelic hosts and all the redeemed of the Lord, join in applauding acclamation at the decision of the Supreme Judge. The heavens (for the earth is no more, it is burnt up) shall declare his righteousness, the exact justice of the whole procedure, where justice alone has been done without partiality, and without severity, nor could it be otherwise, for God is Judge himself. Thus the assembly is dissolved; the righteous are received into everlasting glory, and the wicked turned into hell, with all those who forget God. Some think that the sentence against the wicked is that which is contained, <reference osisRef="Psa.50.16-Psa.50.22">Psa 50:16-22</reference>. See the analysis at the end, and particularly on the six first verses, in which a somewhat different view of the subject is taken.
entries.fba1dd8929c2a41812169cef98b8a0acccc2b3aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20224" type="x-p"/> Hear, O my people - As they were now amply informed concerning the nature and certainty of the general judgment, and were still in a state of probation, Asaph proceeds to show them the danger to which they were exposed, and the necessity of repentance and amendment, that when that great day should arrive, they might be found among those who had made a covenant with God by sacrifice. And he shows them that the sacrifice with which God would be well pleased was quite different from the bullocks, he-goats, etc., which they were in the habit of offering. In short, he shows here that God has intended to abrogate those sacrifices, as being no longer of any service: for when the people began to trust in them, without looking to the thing signified, it was time to put them away. When the people began to pay Divine honors to the brazen serpent, though it was originally an ordinance of God's appointment for the healing of the Israelites, it was ordered to be taken away; called nehushtan, a bit of brass; and broken to pieces. The sacrifices under the Jewish law were of God's appointment; but now that the people began to put their trust in them, God despised them.
entries.f0db7654bfbb8ba830cd36413e61fba4f6c0f012: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20225" type="x-p"/> I will not reprove thee - I do not mean to find fault with you for not offering sacrifices; you have offered them, they have been continually before me: but you have not offered them in the proper way.
entries.06ec5dcb43d14f74e0c67c2e6a763436b1f6b623: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen20225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20226" type="x-p"/> Every beast of the forest is mine - Can ye suppose that ye are laying me under obligation to you, when ye present me with a part of my own property?
entries.456946eeb4572a34af482111811d2a400e891d41: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen20226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20227" type="x-p"/> The world is mine, and the fullness thereof - Ye cannot, therefore, give me any thing that is not my own.
entries.e22b73c0dc8db8e7744e41018d536549efec7469: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen20227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20228" type="x-p"/> Will I eat the flesh of bulls - Can ye be so simple as to suppose that I appointed such sacrifices for my own gratification? All these were significative of a spiritual worship, and of the sacrifice of that Lamb of God which, in the fullness of time, was to take away, in an atoning manner, the sin of the world.
entries.e3d2770927355d45dc25ddcf258c4a011d55e722: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen20228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20229" type="x-p"/> Offer unto God thanksgiving; and pay thy vows unto the Most High - זבח zebach, "sacrifice unto God, אלהים Elohim, the תודה todah, thank-offering," which was the same as the sin-offering, viz. a bullock, or a ram, without blemish; only there were, in addition, "unleavened cakes mingled with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil; and cakes of fine flour mingled with oil and fried," <reference osisRef="Lev.7.12">Lev 7:12</reference>. <div eID="gen20229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20230" type="x-p"/> And pay thy vows - נדריך nedareycha, "thy vow-offering, to the Most High." The neder or vow-offering was a male without blemish, taken from among the beeves, the sheep, or the goats. Compare <reference osisRef="Lev.22.19">Lev 22:19</reference> with <reference osisRef="Psa.50.22">Psa 50:22</reference>. Now these were offerings, in their spiritual and proper meaning, which God required of the people: and as the sacrificial system was established for an especial end - to show the sinfulness of sin, and the purity of Jehovah, and to show how sin could be atoned for, forgiven, and removed; this system was now to end in the thing that it signified, - the grand sacrifice of Christ, which was to make atonement, feed, nourish, and save the souls of believers unto eternal life; to excite their praise and thanksgiving; bind them to God Almighty by the most solemn vows to live to him in the spirit of gratitude and obedience all the days of their life. And, in order that they might be able to hold fast faith and a good conscience, they were to make continual prayer to God, who promised to hear and deliver them, that they might glorify him, <reference osisRef="Psa.50.15">Psa 50:15</reference>. <div eID="gen20230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20231" type="x-p"/> From the <reference osisRef="Psa.50.16">Psa 50:16</reference> to the <reference osisRef="Psa.50.22">Psa 50:22</reference> Asaph appears to refer to the final rejection of the Jews from having any part in the true covenant sacrifice.
entries.e74c13d02adb00552c73e9ff26f302377948bacf: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen20231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20232" type="x-p"/> But unto the wicked - The bloodthirsty priests, proud Pharisees, and ignorant scribes of the Jewish people.
entries.72139bb7feb4bf5202c21d77532bb46d932a28e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen20232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20233" type="x-p"/> Seeing thou hatest instruction - All these rejected the counsel of God against themselves; and refused to receive the instructions of Christ.
entries.c3e62fbaeaa92c14483e031b33a20dddcbc64467: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen20233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20234" type="x-p"/> When thou sawest a thief - Rapine, adulteries, and adulterous divines, were common among the Jews in our Lord's time. The Gospels give full proof of this.
entries.e6c0b92b86d29d89d11086382a762ed282c158be: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen20234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20235" type="x-p"/> These things hast thou done - My eye has been continually upon you, though my judgments have not been poured out: and because I was silent, thou didst suppose I was such as thyself; but I will reprove thee, etc. I will visit for these things.
entries.2082c94bb46b2d006e180f909cfa523e050b9d00: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen20235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20236" type="x-p"/> Now consider this - Ye have forgotten your God, and sinned against him. He has marked down all your iniquities, and has them in order to exhibit against you. Beware, therefore, lest he tear you to pieces, when there is none to deliver; for none can deliver you but the Christ you reject. And how can ye escape, if ye neglect so great a salvation?
entries.ed7012b6768a2426916d32e1d1b3e9aa9bda601e: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen20236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20237" type="x-p"/> Whoso offereth praise - These are the very same words as those in <reference osisRef="Psa.50.14">Psa 50:14</reference>, זבח תודה; and should be read the same way independently of the points, zebach todah, "sacrifice the thank-offering." Jesus is the great eucharistic sacrifice; offer him up to God in your faith and prayers. By this sacrifice is God glorified, for in him is God well pleased; and it was by the grace or good pleasure of God that he tasted death for every man. <div eID="gen20237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20238" type="x-p"/> Ordereth his conversation - שם דרך sam derech, Disposeth his way. - Margin. Has his way There, שם דרך sham derech, as many MSS. and old editions have it; or makes that his custom. <div eID="gen20238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20239" type="x-p"/> Will I show the salvation of God - אראנו arennu, I will cause him to see בישע beyesha, into the salvation of God; into God's method of saving sinners by Christ. He shall witness my saving power even to the uttermost; such a salvation as it became a God to bestow, and as a fallen soul needs to receive; the salvation from all sin, which Christ has purchased by his death. I sall scheu til him, the hele of God; that es Jeshu, that he se him in the fairehed of his majeste - Old Psalter.  <chapter eID="Ps.50"/> <div eID="gen20239" type="x-p"/>

entries.bfb3a78590c21d5bd409fe052c95127d7d738e5c: <div eID="gen9510" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Divine Discourse concerning the True Sacrifice and Worship</title> <div sID="gen9511" type="x-p"/> With the preceding Psalm the series of the Korahitic Elohim-Psalms of the primary collection (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>) closes. There are, reckoning <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1-Ps.42.11">Psa 42:1-11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.43.1-Ps.43.5">Psa 43:1-5</reference> as one Psalm, seven of them (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.1">Psa 42:1</reference>). They form the principal group of the Korahitic Psalms, to which the third book furnishes a supplement, bearing in part an Elohimic (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.1-Ps.84.12">Psa 84:1-12</reference>) and in part a Jehovic impress (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.1-Ps.85.13">Psa 85:1-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.87.1-Ps.88.18">Ps 87:1-88:18</reference>). The Asaphic Psalms, on the contrary, belong exclusively to the Elohimic style of Psalms, but do not, however, all stand together: the principal group of them is to be found in the third book (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.1">Psa 73:1</reference>), and the primary collection contains only one of them, viz., Ps 50, which is here placed immediately after Ps 49 on account of several points of mutual relationship, and more especially because the prominent <hi type="italic">Hear then, My people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.7">Psa 50:7</reference>), is in accord with the beginning of Ps 49, <hi type="italic">Hear, all ye peoples.</hi> <div eID="gen9511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9512" type="x-p"/> According to <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.2-1Chr.23.5">1Ch 23:2-5</reference>, the whole of the thirty-eight thousand Levites were divided by David into four divisions (24,000 + 6000 + 4000 + 4000). To the fourth division (4000) was assigned the music belonging to divine worship. Out of this division, however, a select company of two hundred and eighty-eight singers was further singled out, and divided into twenty-four classes. These last were placed under three leaders or precentors (<hi type="italic">Sangmeister</hi>), viz., fourteen classes under Heman the Kehathite and this fourteen sons; four classes under Asaph the Gersonite and his four sons; and six classes under Ethan (Jeduthun) and his six sons (1 Chr. 25, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.15.1-Ps.15.5">Psa 15:1-5</reference> :17ff.). The instruments played by these three leaders, which they made use of on account of their clear, penetrating sound, were the cymbals (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19">1Ch 15:19</reference>). Also in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.5">1Ch 16:5</reference>, where Asaph is described as the chief (הראשׁ) of the sacred music in the tent where the Ark was placed, he strikes the cymbals. That he was the chief, first leader, cannot be affirmed. The usual order of the names if “Heman, Asaph, and Ethan.” The same order is also observed in the genealogies of the three in 1 Chron 6:16-32. Heman takes the prominent place, and at his right hand stands Asaph, and on his left Ethan. History bears witness to the fact that Asaph was also a Psalm-writer. For, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.30">2Ch 29:30</reference>, Hezekiah brought “the words of David and of Asaph the seer” into use again in the service of the house of God. And in the Book of Nehemiah, <reference osisRef="Neh.12.46">Neh 12:46</reference>, David and Asaph are placed side by side as ראשׁי המּשׁררים in the days of old in Israel. <div eID="gen9512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9513" type="x-p"/> The twelve Psalms bearing the inscription לאסף are all Elohimic. The name of God יהוה does not occur at all in two (Ps 77, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.1-Ps.82.8">Psa 82:1-8</reference>), and in the rest only once, or at the most twice. Side by side with אלהים, אדני and אל are used as favourite names, and especial preference is also given to עליון. Of compounded names of God, אל אלהים והוה (only besides in <reference osisRef="Josh.22.22">Jos 22:22</reference>) in the Psalter, and אלהים צבאות in the Old Testament Scriptures generally (vid., <hi type="italic">Symbolae</hi>, pp. 14-16), are exclusively peculiar to them. So far as concerns their contents, they are distinguished from the Korahitic Psalms by their prophetically judicial character. As in the prophets, God is frequently introduced as speaking; and we meet with detailed prophetical pictures of the appearing of God the Judge, together with somewhat long judicial addresses (Ps 50; <reference osisRef="Ps.75.1-Ps.75.10">Psa 75:1-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.82.1-Ps.82.8">Psa 82:1-8</reference>). The appellation החזה, which Asaph bears in <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.30">2Ch 29:30</reference>, accords with this; notwithstanding the chronicler also applies the same epithet to both the other precentors. The ground of this, as with נבּא, which is used by the chronicler of the singing and playing of instruments in the service of the house of God, is to be found in the intimate connection between the sacred lyric and prophecy as a whole. The future visionary character of the Asaphic Psalms has its reverse side in the historical past. We frequently meet with descriptive retrospective glances at facts of the primeval history (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.13-Ps.74.15">Psa 74:13-15</reference>; Psa 77:15., <reference osisRef="Ps.80.9-Ps.80.12">Psa 80:9-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.81.5-Ps.81.8">Psa 81:5-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.83.10-Ps.83.12">Psa 83:10-12</reference>), and Ps 78 is entirely taken up with holding up the mirror of the ancient history of the nation to the people of the present. If we read the twelve Psalms of Asaph in order one after the other, we shall, moreover, observe this striking characteristic, that mention is made of Joseph and the tribes descended from him more frequently than anywhere else (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.16">Psa 77:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.9">Psa 78:9</reference>, Psa 78:67., <reference osisRef="Ps.81.6">Psa 81:6</reference>; Psa 80:2.). Nor is another feature less remarkable, viz., that the mutual relationship of Jahve to Israel is set forth under the figure of the shepherd and his flock rather than any other (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.1">Psa 74:1</reference>; 77:21; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.52">Psa 78:52</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.70-Ps.78.72">Psa 78:70-72</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.79.13">Psa 79:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.2">Psa 80:2</reference>). Moreover these Psalms delight in other respects to vary the designations for the people of God as much as possible. <div eID="gen9513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9514" type="x-p"/> In Ps 50, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.1">Psa 73:1</reference>, we have before us a peculiar type of Psalms. The inscription לאסף has, so to speak, deep-lying internal grounds in its support. But it does not follow from this inscription that all these Psalms were composed by the aged Asaph, who, as <reference osisRef="Ps.78.69">Psa 78:69</reference> shows, lived until the early part of Solomon’s reign. The outward marks peculiar to Asaph were continued in his posterity even into the period after the Exile. History mentions Asaphites under Jehoshaphat (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.14">2Ch 20:14</reference>), under Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.29.13">2Ch 29:13</reference>), and among the exiles who returned (Ezr 2:41, cf. Ezr 3:10, one hundred and twenty-eight Asaphites; <reference osisRef="Neh.7.44">Neh 7:44</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Neh.11.22">Neh 11:22</reference>, a hundred and forty-eight of them). Since down to the period after the Exile even the cymbals (מצלתּים) descended to them from their ancestor, the poetic talent and enthusiasm may also have been hereditary among them. The later “Psalms of Asaph,” whether composed by later Asaphites or some other person, are inscribed לאסף because, by whomsoever, they are composed in the style of Asaph and after Asaphic models. Ps 50, however, is an original Psalm of Asaph. <div eID="gen9514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9515" type="x-p"/> After the manner of the prophets the twofold truth is here advanced, that God has no delight in animal sacrifice without the sacrifice of prayer in which the heart is engaged, and that the confession of His word without a life that accords with His word is an abomination to Him. It is the very same fundamental thought which is expressed in <reference osisRef="Ps.40.7-Ps.40.9">Psa 40:7-9</reference>; Psa 69:31., Psa 51:18., and underlies <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1-Ps.24.10">Psa 24:1-10</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>) and <reference osisRef="Ps.15.1">Psa 15:1</reference>; they are all echoes of the grand utterance of Samuel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>), the father of the poetry of the Psalms. It cannot surprise one that stress is laid on this denunciation of a heartless service of works by so many voices during the Davidic age. The nothingness of the <hi type="italic">opus operatum</hi> is also later on the watchword of the prophets in times when religious observances, well ordered and in accordance with legal prescription, predominate in Judah. Nor should it seem strange that Asaph the Levite, who was appointed to the sanctuary on Zion, expresses himself thus; for Jeremiah was also a Levite and even a priest (<hi type="italic">cohen</hi>), and yet no one has spoken a bolder, and more cutting word against the outward and formal service of sacrifice than he (Jer 7:22.). Both these objections being removed, there is nothing else that stands in the way of our ascribing this Psalm to Asaph himself. This is favoured by echoes of the Psalm in the prophets (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.50.2">Psa 50:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">Lam 2:15</reference>, and the verse-ending <reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">Psa 50:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.18">Psa 38:18</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.49.16">Isa 49:16</reference>), and there is nothing opposed to it in the form of the language.
entries.6a4ebfdf1527ec14d26a8abbabc18a14ae3ae038: <reference osisRef="Ps.50.1-Ps.50.3">Psa 50:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9516" type="x-p"/> The theophany. The names of God are heaped up in <reference osisRef="Ps.50.1">Psa 50:1</reference> in order to gain a thoroughly full-toned exordium for the description of God as the Judge of the world. Hupfeld considers this heaping up cold and stiff; but it is exactly in accordance with the taste of the Elohimic style. The three names are co-ordinate with one another; for אל אלהים does not mean “God of gods,” which would rather be expressed by אלהי האלהים or אל אלים. אל is the name for God as the Almighty; אלהים as the Revered One; יהוה as the Being, absolute in His existence, and who accordingly freely influences and moulds history after His own plan - this His peculiar proper-name is the third in the triad. Perfects alternate in <reference osisRef="Ps.50.1">Psa 50:1</reference> with futures, at one time the idea of that which is actually taking place, and at another of that which is future, predominating. Jahve summons the earth to be a witness of the divine judgment upon the people of the covenant. The addition “from the rising of the sun to its going down,” shows that the poet means the earth in respect of its inhabitants. He speaks, and because what He speaks is of universal significance He makes the earth in all its compass His audience. This summons precedes His self-manifestation. It is to be construed, with Aquila, the Syriac, Jerome, Tremellius, and Montanus, “out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, Elohim shineth.” Zion, the perfect in beauty (cf. the dependent passage <reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">Lam 2:15</reference>, and 1 Macc. 2:12, where the temple is called ἡ καλλονὴ ἡμῶν), because the place of the presence of God the glorious One, is the bright spot whence the brightness of the divine manifestation spreads forth like the rising sun. In itself certainly it is not inappropriate, with the lxx, Vulgate, and Luther, to take מכלל־יפי as a designation of the manifestation of Elohim in His glory, which is the <hi type="italic">non pius ultra</hi> of beauty, and consequently to be explained according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.12">Eze 28:12</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.33.19">Exo 33:19</reference>, and not according to <reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">Lam 2:15</reference> (more particularly since Jeremiah so readily gives a new turn to the language of older writers). But, taking the fact into consideration that nowhere in Scripture is beauty (יפי) thus directly predicated of God, to whom peculiarly belongs a glory that transcends all beauty, we must follow the guidance of the accentuation, which marks מכלל־יפי by <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> as in apposition with ציּון (cf. <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 49; tr. p. 60). The poet beholds the appearing of God, an appearing that resembles the rising of the sun (הופיע, as in the Asaph <reference osisRef="Ps.80.2">Psa 80:2</reference>, after <reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">Deu 33:2</reference>, from יפע, with a transition of the primary notion of rising, Arab. <hi type="italic">yf‛</hi>, <hi type="italic">wf‛</hi>, to that of beaming forth and lighting up far and wide, as in Arab. <hi type="italic">sṭ‛</hi>); for “our God will come and by no means keep silence.” It is not to be rendered: Let our God come (Hupfeld) and not keep silence (Olshausen). The former wish comes too late after the preceding הופיע (יבא is consequently <hi type="italic">veniet</hi>, and written as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.13">Psa 37:13</reference>), and the latter is superfluous. אל, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.34.6">Psa 34:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.41.3">Psa 41:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.9">Isa 2:9</reference>, and frequently, implies in the negative a lively interest on the part of the writer: He cannot, He dare not keep silence, His glory will not allow it. He who gave the Law, will enter into judgment with those who have it and do not keep it; He cannot long look on and keep silence. He must punish, and first of all by word in order to warn them against the punishment by deeds. Fire and storm are the harbingers of the Lawgiver of Sinai who now appears as Judge. The fire threatens to consume the sinners, and the storm (viz., a tempest accompanied with lightning and thunder, as in <reference osisRef="Job.38.1">Job 38:1</reference>) threatens to drive them away like chaff. The expression in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.50.3">Psa 50:3</reference></hi> is like Psa 18:9. The <hi type="italic">fem</hi>. <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נשׂערה does not refer to אשׁ, but is used as neuter: it is stormed, i.e., a storm rages (Apollinaris, ἐλαιλαπίσθη σφόδρα). The fire is His wrath; and the storm the power or force of His wrath.
entries.e69b19ee9b7c6d3347eea482a2df29b9b9995911: <reference osisRef="Ps.50.4-Ps.50.6">Psa 50:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen9516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9517" type="x-p"/> The judgment scene. To the heavens above (מעל, elsewhere a preposition, here, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.27.39">Gen 27:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.49.25">Gen 49:25</reference>, an adverb, <hi type="italic">desuper , superne</hi>) and to the earth God calls (קרא אל, as, e.g., <reference osisRef="Gen.28.1">Gen 28:1</reference>), to both לדין עמּו, in order to sit in judgment upon His people in their presence, and with them as witnesses of His doings. Or is it not that they are summoned to attend, but that the commission, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.5">Psa 50:5</reference>, is addressed to them (Olshausen, Hitzig)? Certainly not, for the act of gathering is not one that properly belongs to the heavens and the earth, which, however, because they exist from the beginning and will last for ever, are suited to be witnesses (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.26">Deu 4:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.1">Deu 32:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Isa 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.1">1</reference> Macc. 2:37). The summons אספוּ is addressed, as in <reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">Mat 24:31</reference>, and frequently in visions, to the celestial spirits, the servants of the God here appearing. The accused who are to be brought before the divine tribunal are mentioned by names which, without their state of mind and heart corresponding to them, express the relationship to Himself in which God has placed them (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">Deu 32:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.19">Isa 42:19</reference>). They are called חסידים, as in the Asaph Psa 79:2. This contradiction between their relationship and their conduct makes an undesigned but bitter irony. In a covenant relationship, consecrated and ratified by a covenant sacrifice (עלי־זבח similar to <reference osisRef="Ps.92.4">Psa 92:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.10">Psa 10:10</reference>), has God placed Himself towards them (Ex 24); ); and this covenant relationship is also maintained on their part by offering sacrifices as an expression of their obedience and of their fidelity. The participle כּרתי here implies the constant continuance of that primary covenant-making. Now, while the accused are gathered up, the poet hears the heavens solemnly acknowledge the righteousness of the Judge beforehand. The participial construction שׁפט הוּא, which always, according to the connection, expresses the present (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.2">Nah 1:2</reference>), or the past (Jdg 4:4), or the future (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.31">Jer 25:31</reference>), is in this instance an expression of that which is near at hand (<hi type="italic">fut. instans</hi>). הוּא has not the sense of <hi type="italic">ipse</hi> (Ew. §314, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), for it corresponds to the “I” in אני שׁפט or הנני שׁפט; and כּי is not to be translated by <hi type="italic">nam</hi> (Hitzig), for the fact that God intends to judge requires no further announcement. On the contrary, because God is just now in the act of sitting in judgment, the heavens, the witnesses most prominent and nearest to Him, bear witness to His righteousness. The earthly music, as the סלה directs, is here to join in with the celestial praise. Nothing further is now wanting to the completeness of the judgment scene; the action now begins.
entries.6093799ea37055eae337f74dc842a0e827fa74a0: <reference osisRef="Ps.50.7-Ps.50.15">Psa 50:7-15</reference> <div eID="gen9517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9518" type="x-p"/> Exposition of the sacrificial Tôra for the good of those whose holiness consists in outward works. The forms strengthened by <hi type="italic">ah</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Ps.50.7">Psa 50:7</reference>, describe God’s earnest desire to have Israel for willing hearers as being quite as strong as His desire to speak and to bear witness. העיד בּ, <hi type="italic">obtestari aliquem</hi>, to come forward as witness, either solemnly assuring, or, as here and in the Psalm of Asaph, <reference osisRef="Ps.81.9">Psa 81:9</reference>, earnestly warning and punishing (cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">šahida</hi> with <hi type="italic">b</hi>, to bear witness against any one). On the <hi type="italic">Dagesh forte conjunctive</hi> in בּך, vid., Ges. §20, 2, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. He who is speaking has a right thus to stand face to face with Israel, for he is Elohim, the God of Israel - by which designation reference is made to the words אנכי יהוה אלהיך (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.2">Exo 20:2</reference>), with which begins the Law as given from Sinai, and which here take the Elohimic form (whereas in <reference osisRef="Ps.81.11">Psa 81:11</reference> they remain unaltered) and are inverted in accordance with the context.
